questions.q: Why can't an overnight batch job play any role in scoring transactions for this fraud detector?
options: By the time a batch job would run, the fraudulent transaction has already been approved — the score is needed before approval, in hundreds of milliseconds
Batch jobs are always more accurate than streaming jobs
The processor doesn't generate enough data for batch processing
Batch jobs cannot read from event logs
questions.explain: The latency budget is measured in hundreds of milliseconds, ruling out any design with a batch stage in the critical path.

questions.q: Why is this fraud detector a clean fit for Kappa architecture rather than Lambda?
options: There's no separate batch layer needed — every transaction is scored once, live, by one streaming pipeline, with rule changes handled by replaying history
Kappa architecture requires a fraud detector by definition
Lambda architecture cannot process financial transactions
Kappa is simply the newer of the two architectures
questions.explain: There's no slower, 'exact' batch score that would ever replace the real-time one — a hallmark of when Kappa fits better than Lambda.

questions.q: What does the 90-day raw event retention requirement in the scoping numbers directly support?
options: Kappa architecture's requirement for a durable, replayable event source
Reducing the throughput floor needed at peak
Eliminating the need for a serving layer
Meeting the sub-second latency budget
questions.explain: Kappa's reprocessing case — backtesting a changed scoring rule — depends on being able to replay historical events, which requires durable retention.

questions.q: Why does this lesson call a slow serving-layer response "not a performance nitpick" in this context?
options: A response that misses the latency budget effectively approves a transaction it should have flagged as fraud
Slow responses only affect reporting dashboards, not transactions
The serving layer only matters for historical queries
Latency has no effect on fraud outcomes
questions.explain: Because scoring happens before approval, a late answer functionally means the fraud check never happened in time.

questions.q: Which non-functional requirement, beyond throughput and latency, does the kickoff call out as shaping the whole design from the start?
options: Idempotency — never scoring, or alerting on, the same transaction twice
Supporting multiple currencies
Storing transactions in a relational database specifically
Requiring manual review of every transaction
questions.explain: The requirement to never double-score a transaction is called out at kickoff, even though the actual alerting logic that depends on it isn't built until Lesson 77.
